samples.text:
Nowadays, it is quite common to see adults who go back to study at college or university after many years of working. In this essay I will explain the reasons why they do this and the problems which they may face.

There are several reasons why adults decide to return to education. Firstly, many people want to get a better job or a promotion. For example, a person who work in an office for ten years may need a degree in management to become a manager. Secondly, the job market is changing very fast, so some workers have to learn new skills like computer programming, otherwise they can lose their job. Also, some adults did not have chance to study when they were young because their family was poor, so they want to achieve their dream now.

However, adult learners can face many difficulties. The first problem is time. Most adults have full-time job and a family, so it is hard to find time for attending classes and doing homework. For instance, a mother with two children may only study late at night when she is very tired. Another difficulty is money, because courses can be expensive and they may have to pay by themself. In addition, some older students feel nervous to study with younger people and they think they are not so good at using technology.

In conclusion, adults return to education mainly for better career and to learn new skills or to follow an old dream. But they can face problems such as lack of time, money and confidence. I think that if they are well organised, these difficulties can be overcome.
samples.why: Answers both questions with relevant reasons and difficulties · ideas stay fairly general · mechanical linking (Firstly, Also) · adequate vocabulary · several errors in agreement, articles and word form that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
A growing number of people are choosing to resume their studies in their thirties, forties or even later. This essay will examine the main motivations behind this decision and the obstacles that mature students commonly encounter.

The most common reason adults re-enter education is to improve their career prospects. In many industries, qualifications that were sufficient twenty years ago are no longer enough, and employees who wish to be promoted or change profession often need a formal certificate. A nurse, for example, might take a part-time degree in order to move into a management role. Apart from professional motives, some people return to education simply for personal fulfilment. Those who left school early because of financial pressure may feel that they missed an opportunity, and completing a course later in life can give them a strong sense of achievement.

Nevertheless, returning to study as an adult is rarely straightforward. The most obvious challenge is balancing academic work with existing responsibilities. Unlike younger students, most mature learners have jobs, children or elderly parents to look after, which leaves them with limited time and energy for reading and assignments. Financial pressure is another issue, since tuition fees must often be paid while supporting a family, and reducing working hours may not be an option. Finally, some adults lack confidence after a long period away from the classroom. They may feel that their study skills are out of date or worry that they will not keep up with younger classmates, particularly when courses rely heavily on unfamiliar digital tools.

In conclusion, adults go back to education mainly to advance their careers and to fulfil personal ambitions. However, they have to overcome considerable difficulties, including limited time, financial strain and a lack of self-confidence, and they deserves flexible support from colleges and employers.
samples.why: Both questions answered clearly with extended, supported points · clear central idea in each paragraph · good range of linking · some less common collocations · mostly error-free with one minor agreement slip.

samples.text:
Lifelong learning, once regarded as unusual, has become an increasingly familiar pattern, with many people enrolling on courses long after they have left school. Their reasons tend to be both practical and personal, but the path back into education is often complicated by commitments and anxieties that younger students rarely face.

Economic change is perhaps the strongest driving force. As automation and new technologies reshape the labour market, skills that once guaranteed secure employment can quickly become obsolete, and workers who wish to remain employable may have little choice but to retrain. Someone who has spent fifteen years in retail, for instance, might study accounting or data analysis to move into a more stable sector. Yet not every decision is driven by necessity. For many, returning to education is a matter of unfinished business: they may have abandoned their studies to support a family or to start earning, and a degree taken in middle age represents a goal finally achieved rather than a mere qualification.

The difficulties these learners face are, however, considerable. Time is the most pressing constraint, as coursework has to be fitted around full-time jobs, childcare and household responsibilities, often leaving study for late evenings or weekends. This juggling act can be exhausting, and it is one of the main reasons mature students withdraw before completing their courses. Money presents a further obstacle, because fees must usually be met from a household budget that is already stretched, and cutting working hours to study is a luxury few can afford. Less visible, but equally significant, is the psychological barrier. Adults who have not written an essay for decades may doubt their abilities and feel out of place among classmates half their age.

In short, adults return to education to keep pace with a changing economy and to fulfil long-held aspirations. Although lack of time, financial pressure and self-doubt can make the experience demanding, these obstacles are far easier to overcome when institutions offer flexible timetables and targeted support.
samples.why: Fully addresses both questions with well-developed, logically sequenced ideas · skilful cohesion · precise, natural vocabulary (obsolete, unfinished business, juggling act) · wide range of accurate complex structures.
